title: Reducing the acoustical façade load from road traffic with green roofs
research_question: To numerically investigate the influence of a green roof on the façade noise load from road traffic at close distance.

participants.description: Numerical simulations of sound propagation in idealized building configurations.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Configuration 1: Terrace extension of a main building, with a green roof on the terrace. Two lengths considered: 5 m and 10 m. Road located at 5 m or 10 m from façade A. Façade B (window at y=3-5m) is the receiver façade. Roofs are either rigid or green (extensive/intensive, various depths: 5 cm, 10 cm, 20 cm).

Configuration 2: Idealized street canyon with three buildings. The middle building's roof is either rigid or green (extensive/intensive, various depths: 10 cm, 20 cm). Roof slopes considered: 0° (flat), 15°, 30°, 45°. Road traffic source is located in the street on the left side of the middle building. Façade C (receiver façade) is on the right building.

Road traffic noise, simulated using the Harmonoise/Imagine source model. Light vehicles (type 1) and heavy vehicles (type 3) were considered. Driving speeds ranged from 30 km/h to 130 km/h (in steps of 10 km/h). Source heights: 0.01m (rolling noise) and 0.30m/0.75m (engine noise).

measures.instrument: Numerical simulation using Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) method with Harmonoise/Imagine source model

measures.construct: Sound pressure level relative to rigid roof
measures.instrument: Numerical simulation using Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) method with Harmonoise/Imagine source model

findings.consequent: Façade noise load at non-directly exposed (parts of) façades
findings.mechanism: Green roofs are porous and thus allow sound to enter the growing mediums. Because of the large number of interactions between sound and substrate particles, attenuation occurs. Moreover, the modified sound waves can destructively interfere at locations where quietness is desired.
findings.quote: Consistent positive effects of the presence of a green roof are observed at non-directly exposed (parts of) façades.

findings.consequent: Reduction in total A-weighted road traffic noise level
findings.quote: A sufficient green roof area is needed to obtain significant reductions in total A-weighted road traffic noise level.

findings.mechanism: At low speeds, engine noise (low frequencies) is dominant. At higher speeds, high-frequency rolling noise becomes more important. The impedance of the green roof substrate decreases with frequency, increasing absorption.
findings.quote: With increasing traffic speed, the green roof effect increases for light vehicles.

findings.mechanism: Low-frequency dominated engine noise has an important contribution at all speeds for heavy vehicles. Engine is located at a higher position, resulting in a smaller acoustical shadow zone.
findings.quote: In case of heavy vehicles, this dependence is less strong.

findings.mechanism: Direct sound is dominant once outside the diffraction zone caused by the extension.
findings.quote: The effect of the presence of a green roof, relative to a rigid roof, is small in the case of an extension of 5 m.

findings.antecedent: Green roof on 5m building extension (Configuration 1) with direct view between source and receiver
findings.mechanism: Direct sound is dominant once outside the diffraction zone caused by the extension.
findings.quote: An increase in shielding is only observed when there is no direct view between the source and receivers at the façade.

findings.mechanism: The full façade has no direct view towards the source, even considering heavy traffic engine noise source height.
findings.quote: For the extension of 10 m, positive effects are observed over the full façade height of the building.

findings.antecedent: Green roof surface area (10m vs 5m extension in Configuration 1)
findings.mechanism: Diffracting sound waves interact longer with the green roof before reaching the façade with larger surface area.
findings.quote: The green roof effect... is larger for the 10-m extension than for the 5-m extension.

findings.antecedent: Extensive green roof (5 cm depth) vs other green roof types/depths (Configuration 1, light vehicles)
findings.quote: For light vehicles, only the extensive green roof of 5 cm gives significantly lower positive effects.

findings.antecedent: Green roof type (intensive/extensive) and substrate depth (Configuration 1, 5m extension)
findings.quote: The difference between maximum and minimum effect, when varying substrates, is only 0.5 dBA for light vehicles and 1 dBA for heavy vehicles.

findings.antecedent: Green roof type and substrate depth (Configuration 1, 10m extension, heavy traffic)
findings.quote: For the 10-m building extension, a good choice of green roof characteristics becomes more important, in particular near heavy-traffic dominated roads.

findings.antecedent: Extensive green roof (20 cm depth) vs extensive green roof (10 cm depth) (Configuration 1, heavy vehicles)
findings.mechanism: A thick but highly permeable substrate like the one found in extensive green roofs is beneficial for low-frequency heavy traffic noise.
findings.quote: An extensive green roof of 20 cm... results in an important improvement upon a layer of 10 cm.

findings.antecedent: Substrate thickness of intensive green roofs (Configuration 1, heavy vehicles)
findings.quote: The influence of substrate thickness in case of intensive green roofs is very small for heavy traffic.

findings.antecedent: Roof slope (saddle-backed vs flat) (Configuration 2, rigid roofs)
findings.consequent: Sound pressure levels at façade C
findings.mechanism: The sound propagation problem is very complex, including multiple reflections, multiple diffractions, and interactions between both.
findings.quote: saddle-backed roofs lead in general to higher sound pressure levels at the non-exposed façade than flat roofs.
A flat roof generally results in the best average shielding.
A green roof is especially interesting in case of a saddle-backed roof.

findings.antecedent: Optimized green roof parameters on saddle-backed roof (Configuration 2)
findings.quote: With a good choice of green roof parameters, the shielding of a flat green roof can be approached.

findings.consequent: Sound pressure levels at façade C
findings.quote: The presence of a vegetated roof top largely decreases the sound pressure levels at façade C.

findings.consequent: Sound pressure levels at façade C
findings.quote: For flat roofs, the presence of a green roof results in a shift towards lower sound pressure levels
With increasing height along the façade, there is a general trend towards more shielding by the green roof

findings.antecedent: Green roof on saddle-backed roof vs rigid saddle-backed roof (Configuration 2)
findings.mechanism: The area over which sound waves interact with the green roof during diffraction is larger for non-zero slopes.
findings.quote: For the saddle-backed roofs, the improvement by a green roof relative to a rigid roof is even larger.

findings.antecedent: 30° extensive green roof (20 cm depth) vs 30° rigid roof (Configuration 2, heavy traffic at 70 km/h)
findings.quote: The average difference between a 30° rigid roof and a 30° extensive green roof with a substrate thickness of 20 cm is near 8 dBA

findings.antecedent: 30° extensive green roof (20 cm depth) vs 30° rigid roof (Configuration 2, heavy traffic)
findings.consequent: Maximum noise reduction at façade C
findings.quote: the maximum difference along the façade amounts up to 14 dBA

findings.consequent: Dependence of green roof effect on vehicle speed
findings.mechanism: Sound waves can only reach the receiving canyon by multiple diffractions or by a single diffraction in combination with façade reflections, limiting the increase of the high-frequency component.
findings.quote: The dependence of the green roof effect on vehicle speed is less pronounced in the street canyon configuration than in configuration 1.

findings.consequent: Magnitude of green roof noise reduction effect
findings.quote: The magnitude of the green roof effect is smaller in the street canyon configuration.

mechanisms: Green roofs are porous, allowing sound to enter growing mediums, leading to attenuation through interactions between sound and substrate particles.
Modified sound waves can destructively interfere at desired quiet locations.
The impedance of green roof substrate decreases with frequency, increasing sound absorption at higher frequencies.
For non-zero roof slopes, the area over which sound waves interact with the green roof during diffraction is larger, enhancing shielding.
moderators: Green roof surface area (building extension length)
Direct line of sight between source and receiver
implementation_implications: Roof type and roof coverage are important parameters for the acoustical quality of housings.
These aspects should be considered during building design and city planning, especially when road traffic is situated close to the building façades.
With a good choice of green roof parameters, the shielding of a flat green roof can be approached, particularly for saddle-backed roofs.
limitations: Results apply only to noise produced by a single traffic lane with either light or heavy vehicles, at a constant vehicle speed.
Real-world scenarios involve multilane roads with typical traffic composition and speed distribution.
Quantitative predictions strongly depend on geometrical details of buildings, the building setting, and local road traffic characteristics.
Simulations are limited to 2D, implying an infinitely long (coherent) line source and buildings having a constant cross-section.

mechanism_chain.description: Green roofs reduce the acoustical façade load from road traffic by absorbing and scattering sound waves that would otherwise reflect off or diffract over the roof towards the façade, particularly affecting non-directly exposed parts.

steps.to_construct: Sound waves propagating towards building façade and roof

steps.from_construct: Sound waves interacting with green roof surface (vegetation, substrate)
steps.to_construct: Absorption and scattering of sound energy

steps.from_construct: Reduced sound energy propagating over/around the roof
steps.to_construct: Decreased sound pressure level at non-directly exposed façade sections
